title: Maré: Black Friday without losing a sale
summary: Pages and prices are ready before midnight; a fair line protects checkout; hot deals are split into small piles; two payment providers; checkout does four things; extras switch off first; one screen shows sales per minute.

steps.title: Ready before midnight
steps.caption: Deal pages and prices are prepared days before and served from nearby, so the midnight rush barely touches our own computers.
steps.engineering: Static pages on the CDN with the Black Friday price book pre-rendered and switched on by edge config at 00:00; push notifications go out in cohorts over 10 minutes.
steps.presenterNote: The biggest spike of the night is the one we send ourselves, so we stagger the notifications and prepare every page before midnight.

steps.title: A fair line, not a crash
steps.caption: When checkout is full, new shoppers wait in a short, honest line, and the items in their bag stay reserved while they wait.
steps.engineering: Admission control at a load-tested concurrency limit; signed first-come tokens; the bag reservation is extended while a shopper is queued.
steps.presenterNote: Past a certain point, letting more people in makes checkout slower for everyone. A short line sells more than an error page.

steps.title: Your dress is really yours
steps.caption: Each hot deal is split into small piles, so thousands can grab one at the same moment and nobody buys an item that's already gone.
steps.engineering: Stock split across Redis counters, each decremented atomically with a 20-minute reservation; a Postgres ledger fed by events is the truth; a rebalancer moves units.
steps.presenterNote: Selling the same dress twice means refunds and angry customers for weeks, so we'd rather sell the last few a few seconds later.

steps.title: Two ways to pay
steps.caption: Payments run through two providers. If one starts failing, new payments move to the other within a minute.
steps.engineering: Routing on 1-minute approval rate and response time per acquirer; if fraud scoring slows, it falls back to rules with lower order caps.
steps.presenterNote: On the night, a payment problem is the most expensive failure there is, so there's always a second way to take the money.

steps.title: Checkout does four things
steps.caption: Checkout confirms the item, the price and the payment, saves the order and answers. Warehouse and invoices catch up right after.
steps.engineering: Reservation, price book version, payment authorization, then one transaction with the outbox row; order.v4 consumers autoscale on lag and fall behind safely.
steps.presenterNote: Anything checkout waits for can break it, so it waits for four things and everything else catches up afterwards.

steps.title: Extras switch off first
steps.caption: Under pressure, suggestions and videos switch off first, in an order agreed in October. The buy button never switches off.
steps.engineering: Degradation ladder L0–L4 as feature flags per tier, stepped up by error-budget burn; fallbacks are pre-rendered; L1 is automatic, higher levels need a person.
steps.presenterNote: We decide what to give up while we're calm, not at midnight, and we rehearse it before the night.

steps.title: Sales per minute, live
steps.caption: One screen shows sales per minute against the forecast, so the team sees trouble before customers feel it.
steps.engineering: Order events stream into ClickHouse; a synthetic checkout runs every minute; traces link the browser to the database; fast-burn alerts at 14.4×.
steps.presenterNote: The number everyone watches is sales per minute, because that's what an outage actually costs.
